newsitem.title: USA: SEC official pushes for decimal pricing of stocks.
newsitem.headline: SEC official pushes for decimal pricing of stocks.

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commissioner Steven Wallman told lawmakers Thursday the time is ripe to move stock quoting in the United States to dollars and cents rather than fractions.
"If we wait for a time when nothing is happening in the markets, we will wait forever," Wallman told members of the House Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials.

"While we could continue to study the issue, I doubt we will learn much more than we already know. In the meantime, we know that the studies to date, and the experience of other markets, support moving to decimals as soon as possible," Wallman said.

Last month, subcommittee chairman Michael Oxley, an Ohio Republican, and Massachusetts Democrat Edward Markey introduced legislation that would require the SEC to develop a plan within a year to move stock and options markets away from trading in fractions.

Such a shift would enable investors to save money in transaction costs because there would be a narrower difference between the prices at which they buy and sell stocks, supporters of the legislation say.
Some lawmakers, at the first of two hearings to be held on the legislation, agreed that such a shift is needed.

"The United States is about the only nation still trading stocks in fractions," Oxley said. He called the current system antiquated and noted that it dates back to the 1700s, "when trading was done under an oak tree and one-eighth of a Spanish dollar was the common currency."
However, there were some reservations among members of the congressional panel.

"While it may be inevitable, I would like to better understand the need for Congress and the SEC to intervene," said Representative Thomas Manton, a New York Democrat and the ranking minority member on the subcommittee.

Also echoing concerns raised by the securities industry, Representative Rick Lazio, R.-N.Y., warned that imposing such a move could be highly disruptive to the markets. He said the panel will ask the agency for a study on the proposal.
Investors, including big pension funds and state and local governments, lauded the plan.

"We believe the savings that may be realised by investors is so sizable as to command reform by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the New York Stock Exchange," Bartlett Naylor, of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, told the committee.

Naylor said a switch from fractions to decimals would save Teamster funds $21 million a year. "A survey of our money managers reveals a diversity of views, but most conclude that we will save money and that the sky will not collapse upon Wall Street," he said.
